claims.text: The target eutectic HEA contains a hard intermetallic phase and a ductile matrix.
The hard intermetallic phase and ductile matrix have distinct electrical conductivities at their boundaries.
Sliding wear exposes fresh phase boundaries in the target HEA.
Electrical differences between phases create micro-galvanic cells at phase boundaries.
Phase-associated micro-galvanic coupling accelerates selective dissolution or localized corrosion.
Wear exacerbates micro-galvanic corrosion by repeatedly exposing fresh interfaces.
A thin nanoparticle coating can be deposited specifically at the relevant phase interfaces.
The nanoparticle coating remains thermally stable at approximately 600°C.
The coating reduces electrical and ionic conductivity contrasts across the phase boundaries.
Acting as an electrical insulator or conductivity homogenizer at phase boundaries suppresses localized galvanic effects.
The coated alloy will have fewer localized pits than the matched uncoated alloy.
The coated alloy will have a lower corrosion current density than the matched uncoated alloy.
The nanoparticle coating will leave mechanical wear rate largely unchanged.
Reduced corrosion with little change in wear will produce a lower total degradation rate.
Chloride-containing media can promote localized attack in HEAs.
The proposed mechanism is relevant under simultaneous sliding and chloride-electrolyte exposure at approximately 600°C.
An adherent and intact coating is a required boundary condition for the comparison.
Rapid coating failure resulting in similar or worse degradation would falsify both the proposed dominant micro-galvanic mechanism and the coating's effectiveness.

contradictions.description: The boundary requires the coating to remain adherent and intact, but rapid coating failure is also treated as a result that falsifies the underlying micro-galvanic mechanism. Coating failure violates the stated boundary and can falsify coating effectiveness, but it does not by itself falsify micro-galvanic dominance.
